passages.t: Before Pilate: “I find no basis for a charge”
passages.happening:
The whole council takes Jesus to Pilate. They accuse him: “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar, and proclaiming Himself to be Christ, a King” (verse 2).

Pilate asks him, “Are You the King of the Jews?” “You have said so,” Jesus replies (verse 3). Pilate tells the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no basis for a charge against this man” (verse 4). But they insist: “He stirs up the people all over Judea with His teaching. He began in Galilee and has come all the way here” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. In 1961 a stone found at Caesarea on the coast was seen to bear his name and the title ‘prefect of Judea’ (see the book page). Only the Roman governor could order a crucifixion.

So the charges are put in words a Roman would care about. Not ‘he claims to be the Son of God’, which was the council's question in the night (22:70), but trouble-making, refusing taxes, and claiming to be a king. Luke's reader knows the second charge is false. A few days earlier Jesus had said, in public, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (20:25).

Only Luke gives the charges in this form, and only Luke has Pilate's first verdict here. It is the first of three times in this chapter that Pilate says Jesus is innocent (verses 4, 14-15, 22).
passages.ot: The false charges recall the psalms of the righteous sufferer: “For false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence” (Psalm 27:12). And Isaiah's servant was condemned “although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth” (Isaiah 53:9).
passages.hard: If Pilate found no charge, why did he not set Jesus free? Luke will show the answer in the next scenes: he gave way to pressure. Luke does not excuse him. A judge who knows a man is innocent and condemns him anyway is not innocent himself. Readers differ on how far Luke's picture of a reluctant Pilate is memory and how far it is shaped by Luke's wish to show Roman readers that Jesus was no rebel. Either way, the story is plain that Jesus died an innocent man.
passages.asks: The leaders brought charges that sounded right to the person they needed to persuade. Ask whether you have ever described someone in the worst light to get your way. Jesus did not argue. The truth about him was enough.

passages.t: Before Herod, who wanted a miracle
passages.happening:
When Pilate hears the word Galilee, he asks if Jesus is a Galilean. Learning that Jesus comes under Herod's rule, he sends him to Herod, who is also in Jerusalem at the time (verses 6-7).

Herod is very pleased to see Jesus. He has wanted to see him for a long time, and hopes to see him do a miracle. He questions him at length, but Jesus gives no answer. The chief priests and scribes stand there accusing him fiercely. Then Herod and his soldiers mock him, dress him in a fine robe, and send him back to Pilate (verses 8-11).

“That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this. Herod here is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39. He had imprisoned John the Baptist and later beheaded him (3:19-20; 9:9). When he heard about Jesus, he said, ‘I beheaded John’, and asked, “who is this man I hear such things about?” And “he kept trying to see Jesus” (9:9). Some Pharisees once warned Jesus that Herod wanted to kill him, and Jesus called him “that fox” (13:32). Like many pilgrims, Herod had come up to Jerusalem for the feast.

Now Herod gets what he wanted, and it does him no good. He wants a show. Jesus gives him nothing, not a miracle and not a word. The man who silenced the prophet John hears nothing from the one John pointed to.

The fine robe was mockery: dress the would-be king like a king. Luke does not say why Herod and Pilate had been enemies. He notes only that they became friends over Jesus. In Acts the first Christians remember it in their prayer: Herod and Pontius Pilate joined together against Jesus (Acts 4:27).
passages.ot:
Jesus' silence fits Isaiah's servant: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7).

The early Christians heard Psalm 2 in this scene: “The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2), and they prayed it in Acts 4:25-27.
passages.hard: Why did Jesus not answer Herod? He had answered Pilate, briefly, and he had answered the council. Many readers think the difference lies in Herod. He did not want the truth; he wanted entertainment. Jesus does not do signs on demand for those who only want to watch (11:29). Herod had already heard God's word from John and silenced it. There comes a point where silence is the answer.
passages.asks: Herod wanted to see Jesus for years, but only to see a trick. Ask what you want from Jesus. If it is only something to watch, or a show of power to prove him, you may find him silent. He speaks to those who will listen.

passages.t: Three times innocent, and Barabbas released
passages.happening:
Pilate calls together the chief priests, the rulers and the people. He has examined Jesus and found him not guilty; neither has Herod. “He has done nothing deserving of death. Therefore I will punish Him and release Him” (verses 15-16).

“But they all cried out in unison: ‘Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!’” Barabbas had been put in prison for an uprising in the city, and for murder (verses 18-19). Pilate, wanting to release Jesus, speaks to them again, but they keep shouting, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” (verse 21).

A third time he says, “What evil has this man done? I have found in Him no offense worthy of death” (verse 22). But they keep demanding with loud voices that Jesus be crucified. “And their clamor prevailed” (verse 23). Pilate releases the man imprisoned for insurrection and murder, “and handed Jesus over to their will” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
All four Gospels tell of Barabbas, and the notes on Mark 15:6-15, Matthew 27:15-26 and John 18:39-40 explain it. An ‘insurrection’ means an uprising. Barabbas was the kind of man Rome usually crucified. The name Barabbas is Aramaic and means ‘son of the father’.

Luke counts Pilate's verdicts. Three times he declares Jesus innocent (verses 4, 14-15, 22). Herod finds nothing either (verse 15). One of the criminals on the crosses will say, ‘this man has done nothing wrong’ (verse 41), and the centurion will call him righteous (verse 47). Luke wants no reader to miss it: the one who died was innocent. In Acts Peter says the same to the people of Jerusalem: “You rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be released to you” (Acts 3:14).

‘Punish’ here most likely means a flogging, a Roman whipping. Pilate offers it as a lesser penalty. It is not enough for those shouting.

Verse 17 is missing from the oldest manuscripts, so the Berean Standard Bible, like many modern Bibles, leaves it out.
passages.ot: The innocent one is handed over and the guilty one goes free. Isaiah's servant was “numbered with the transgressors”, and “He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12).
passages.hard:
Who is to blame? Luke names particular people: the chief priests, the rulers, a crowd at the governor's court one morning, Herod, and a Roman governor who knew the truth and gave way. The notes on Matthew 27:15-26 and John 19:13-16 set out in full how Christians for centuries misused these scenes to call the Jewish people ‘Christ-killers’, and they reject that reading completely. Here it is said again, plainly: the Jewish people, then or now, are not guilty of Jesus' death, and this site rejects that charge.

Luke himself shows other Jews in the same chapter: women who mourn for him (verse 27), crowds who go home beating their breasts (verse 48), and Joseph, a member of the council, who did not agree with what was done (verse 51). In Acts the first Christians pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel all stood together against Jesus (Acts 4:27). All people are inside the guilt. And from the cross Jesus prays for those who put him there (verse 34).
passages.asks: ‘Their clamor prevailed.’ Pilate knew what was right, and the noise won. Ask where you have let the loudest voices decide for you, against what you knew. And notice Barabbas: a guilty man walking free because Jesus took his place. Ask whether you can see yourself in him.

passages.t: Simon carries the cross, and the daughters of Jerusalem
passages.happening:
As the soldiers lead Jesus away, they seize Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, and put the cross on him “to carry behind Jesus” (verse 26).

A great crowd follows, including women who are mourning and wailing for him. Jesus turns to them: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children” (verse 28). The days are coming when people will say that women without children are the fortunate ones. People will cry to the mountains to fall on them and to the hills to cover them. “For if men do these things while the tree is green, what will happen when it is dry?” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Roman soldiers could force a civilian to carry a load. Mark names Simon's sons, as if his readers knew them (see the note on Mark 15:21-32). Only Luke says Simon carried the cross ‘behind Jesus’. Many readers hear in it Jesus' own words: “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me” (9:23).

The women and Jesus' words to them are found only in Luke. They are Jewish women of Jerusalem, mourning a Jewish teacher on his way to a Roman cross. Luke does not show a city united against Jesus. He shows a city where many grieve.

Jesus, close to death, turns to comfort and warn them. His words go back to his tears over the city (19:41-44). In that world a woman without children often felt shame and grief; Elizabeth spoke of her ‘disgrace’ (1:25). For a day to come when the childless are called fortunate, the suffering must be terrible. Jesus is thinking of the mothers and children of the city when war comes.
passages.ot:
The cry to the mountains and hills comes from Hosea, who warned of a coming judgment when people “will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us!’ and to the hills, ‘Fall on us!’” (Hosea 10:8). The prophets used such words for days so dreadful that people would rather be buried than see them.

Zechariah had spoken of Jerusalem mourning over one “they have pierced”, mourning “as one mourns for an only child” (Zechariah 12:10).
passages.hard:
What does the green tree and the dry tree mean? It seems to be a proverb, and readers take it in more than one way. Many read it this way: if the Romans do this to an innocent man, who is no rebel, what will they do to a city full of rebels? Others read it of God's judgment: if this is what happens to the innocent one, what will happen to the guilty? Others hear a warning that if people treat Jesus like this while he is among them, things will be worse when he is gone. These notes do not choose. All the readings point to the suffering that came on the city some forty years later (see the note on 19:41-44).

Is this a curse on the women, or on the Jewish people? No. It is a warning spoken in love, by a Jew to the daughters of his own city, as he wept over it a few days before. This is grief, not a verdict.
passages.asks: On the way to his own death, Jesus turned to look after others. Ask whom you are weeping for, and whom you might need to weep for. Grief for Jesus is right, but he points the women to the people around them who are in danger. Ask who that is for you.

passages.t: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”
passages.happening:
Two criminals are led out with Jesus to be executed. At the place called The Skull they crucify him, with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left (verses 32-33).

“Then Jesus said, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ And they divided up His garments by casting lots” (verse 34).

The people stand watching. The rulers sneer: “He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One” (verse 35). The soldiers mock him too, offering him sour wine. Above him hangs a sign: THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels and violent criminals, meant to be slow, public and shameful. The note on Mark 15:21-32 tells more, including the bones of a crucified man found in Jerusalem in 1968, a nail still through the heel. Luke, like Mark, gives none of the physical details. ‘They crucified Him there’ was enough for his readers.

Only Luke gives the prayer. Jesus had taught, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you” (6:27-28). On the cross he does it. In Luke's second book, Stephen, dying under the stones, prays in the same way: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60).

What do the manuscripts show? This prayer is missing from some of the oldest copies of Luke, including a papyrus called P75, copied around AD 200, Codex Vaticanus from the 300s, and Codex Bezae as first written. It is present in Codex Sinaiticus as first written and in most later copies. Scholars are divided. Some think it was added from an early story about Jesus. Others think some scribes left it out because they could not bear the thought of the Jews who rejected Jesus being forgiven. Many modern Bibles print it with a note or in brackets.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's servant “made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12): he prayed for the lawbreakers among whom he was counted. Jesus does exactly that.

Psalm 22 runs through the scene: “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing” (Psalm 22:18), and “All who see me mock me; they sneer and shake their heads” (Psalm 22:7).
passages.hard:
Whom was Jesus praying for? Readers answer in more than one way. Some read ‘them’ as the soldiers who were nailing him and dividing his clothes; they were only following orders and did not know whom they were killing. Some read it as the leaders and the people of Jerusalem too; in Acts Peter tells them, “I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your leaders” (Acts 3:17), and calls them to turn to God. Many read it as everyone who had a part in his death, which in the end means every sinner. These notes do not choose.

Does ‘they do not know’ mean they were not guilty? No. Ignorance does not make a wrong right. But it is the ground of Jesus' plea. He asks his Father to forgive, and Acts shows that forgiveness offered to the very city that cried ‘Crucify’.

One thing is plain, whichever reading is taken. If this prayer is Jesus' own, then no one may use his death to justify hatred of anyone. The one who died prayed for those who killed him. Anyone who uses the cross to stir up contempt for Jews, or for any people, is standing against the prayer of the crucified Lord.
passages.asks: Jesus prayed for his enemies while they were still hurting him, not after they said sorry. Ask whom you find it hardest to pray for. Forgiving does not mean saying the wrong was right, and it does not mean staying where you are in danger. It means handing them to the Father, as Jesus did. You may need to start with his own words.

passages.t: Two criminals, and “today you will be with Me in Paradise”
passages.happening:
One of the criminals hanging there pours abuse on Jesus. “Are You not the Christ?” he says. “Save Yourself and us!” (verse 39).

The other rebukes him: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment? We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve. But this man has done nothing wrong” (verses 40-41).

Then he says, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” (verse 42). And Jesus says to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this. Mark and Matthew say only that both criminals mocked him (Mark 15:32). Luke shows one of them turning.

Look at what the second man does. He fears God. He admits his own guilt, plainly, with no excuses. He says Jesus is innocent. And he asks the dying man beside him to remember him when he comes into his kingdom. Everyone else at the cross mocks ‘king’ as a joke. This man, nailed to a cross, believes it. He brings nothing. He has no time to make anything right. He asks only to be remembered.

Jesus gives him more than he asked. Not ‘someday’, but ‘today’. Not only ‘I will remember you’, but ‘you will be with Me’. ‘Today’ is Luke's word for the moment God's promise arrives: a Savior born today (2:11), salvation come to Zacchaeus' house today (19:9), and now paradise today.

The word Paradise first meant a garden, from an old Persian word for an enclosed park. It came to be used for the place where the righteous dead are with God. In the New Testament it appears only three times: here, where Paul says he “was caught up to Paradise” (2 Corinthians 12:4), and in the promise of “the tree of life in the Paradise of God” (Revelation 2:7).
passages.ot:
The first garden was planted by God himself: “the LORD God planted a garden in Eden” (Genesis 2:8). Humanity was sent out of it. The promise to the criminal is a way back in, through Jesus.

Isaiah's servant was “numbered with the transgressors” and “made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). Here the servant, counted among criminals, brings one of them home.
passages.hard:
Where does the comma go? The oldest Greek manuscripts have little or no punctuation. So some read the sentence, ‘Truly I tell you today, you will be with Me in Paradise’, as a solemn promise made that day, to be kept at the resurrection. Jehovah's Witnesses read it this way in their New World Translation, and so do many Seventh-day Adventists. They hold that the dead sleep until the resurrection, and they note that Jesus said after he rose that he had not yet gone up to the Father (John 20:17).

Most Christians, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, read ‘today’ with what follows, as nearly all English Bibles do. ‘Truly I tell you’ is how Jesus often begins a solemn promise, and he never needs to say which day he is speaking on. ‘Today’ is one of Luke's key words for salvation arriving now. And the man asked about the future, ‘when You come into Your kingdom’; Jesus answers with something sooner. Christians who read it this way still differ on how to describe the time between death and the resurrection, and paradise need not mean the same as Jesus going up to the Father. All agree with the creeds that the final hope is the resurrection of the body.

If you think it is too late for you, this story is for you. A man with hours to live, with nothing to offer, asked to be remembered, and Jesus said ‘today’. But do not read it as a reason to put off turning to God. Only one of the two criminals turned. The other was just as close to Jesus, and mocked. No one is promised the time or the clear mind to turn at the end. The day to answer is today.
passages.asks: Two men hung beside Jesus. One asked for nothing but a miracle, and one asked only to be remembered. Ask which of their prayers sounds more like yours. And if you have been carrying something you think is too bad to bring to Jesus, bring it now. He said ‘today’ to a man who had nothing left.

passages.t: “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit”
passages.happening:
It is about the sixth hour, noon, and darkness comes over the whole land until the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. The sun is darkened, and the veil of the temple is torn down the middle (verses 44-45).

“Then Jesus called out in a loud voice, ‘Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.’ And when He had said this, He breathed His last” (verse 46).

The centurion sees what has happened and gives glory to God: “Surely this was a righteous man” (verse 47). The crowds who came to watch go home beating their breasts. All who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed him from Galilee, stand at a distance, watching (verses 48-49).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell of Jesus' cry, ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’ (see the note on Mark 15:33-39). Luke does not give that cry. His last words of Jesus are a prayer of trust, from the psalms, the prayer of a child to his Father. Both are true of that afternoon, and the Gospels together give both.

The temple had curtains that separated the holy places; the inner one hung before the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went, once a year. Luke tells of the tearing before Jesus dies, Mark after.

A centurion was a Roman officer who commanded a company of soldiers. In Mark he says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (Mark 15:39). In Luke he says, ‘Surely this was a righteous man.’ The Greek word, dikaios, can mean ‘innocent’ or ‘righteous’, and many English Bibles translate it ‘innocent’ here. Luke uses the same word for Simeon (2:25) and for Joseph of Arimathea a few verses later (23:50).

Only Luke tells of the crowds beating their breasts, the gesture of the tax collector in the temple who prayed, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” (18:13). The people of Jerusalem go home grieving.
passages.ot:
Jesus' last words come from Psalm 31:5: “Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth.” Stephen, dying, prays in the same way: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59).

The darkness recalls Amos: “I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime” (Amos 8:9). And the friends standing far off recall the psalm: “my kinsmen stand at a distance” (Psalm 38:11).
passages.hard:
Why does the centurion say ‘righteous’ in Luke and ‘Son of God’ in Mark? Readers explain it in more than one way. Some think Luke chose a word his readers would hear as a verdict: the last of the voices in this chapter declaring Jesus innocent, from Pilate to the criminal to a Roman officer. Some think ‘righteous’ means more than innocent: Jesus is the Righteous One the prophets spoke of, as Peter calls him in Acts 3:14. Many think the two Gospels complete each other: a Roman soldier saw a man die like no one he had seen, and both the innocence and the sonship are true. These notes do not choose.

Did Jesus die in trust or in abandonment? The Gospels give both cries, and Christians hold them together. Jesus truly felt forsaken, as Mark tells, and he died trusting his Father, as Luke tells. If you feel forsaken by God, you can pray as he did, and you should not stay alone with it. Tell someone you trust, and if you are in danger, reach out for help today.
passages.asks: Jesus' last breath was a prayer from the Psalms. Ask what words you would want to have ready for the hardest moment of your life, and whether you could say ‘Father, into Your hands’ now, today, about what frightens you most.

passages.t: Joseph of Arimathea, and the women who saw where he was laid
passages.happening:
There is a man named Joseph, a member of the Council, “a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision or action” (verses 50-51). He comes from the Judean town of Arimathea and is waiting for the kingdom of God. He goes to Pilate and asks for the body of Jesus.

He takes it down, wraps it in a linen cloth, and places it in a tomb cut into the rock, “where no one had yet been laid” (verse 53). It is Preparation Day, and the Sabbath is beginning.

The women who came with Jesus from Galilee follow. They see the tomb and how his body is laid. Then they go home and prepare spices and perfumes. “And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment” (verse 56).
passages.hearers:
All four Gospels tell of Joseph, and the notes on Mark 15:40-47 and John 19:38-42 explain the burial. The Sabbath began at sunset on Friday, and the Law said the body of an executed man must not be left hanging overnight. So the burial had to be done quickly. Wealthier families cut tombs into the rock outside the city. A body was laid inside, and the entrance was closed with a large stone.

Luke tells us two things about Joseph that the others do not. He had not agreed with the council's decision. Not every member of the council was against Jesus. And he was ‘waiting for the kingdom of God’, like old Simeon, who was ‘waiting for the consolation of Israel’ (2:25), and Anna, who spoke to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:38). Luke's book began with faithful Jews waiting for God to act. It ends its story of the cross with another.

The women saw the tomb and how the body was placed. In the next chapter they will be the first to find it empty. They did not go to the wrong tomb. And Luke notes that they kept the Sabbath ‘according to the commandment’. The first witnesses of the resurrection were faithful Jewish women who kept God's Law.
passages.ot:
The Law said: “you must not leave the body on the tree overnight, but you must be sure to bury him that day” (Deuteronomy 21:23).

Isaiah's servant “was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death” (Isaiah 53:9). Matthew says Joseph was a rich man (Matthew 27:57).

The Sabbath rest goes back to the commandment: “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:8).
passages.hard:
Why does Luke stress that the tomb was new, ‘where no one had yet been laid’? Many readers think it matters for what comes next. There could be no mix-up about whose body was missing. It also fits a pattern in Luke: Jesus rode into the city on a colt ‘on which no one has ever sat’ (19:30), and he is laid in a tomb where no one had lain. What is given to him is fresh and set apart.

Why did a council member do this? It cost Joseph something to ask a Roman governor for the body of a man executed as a would-be king. It meant siding with Jesus openly, when the disciples had fled. Some who seem to be far from Jesus turn out, at the hardest moment, to be near.
passages.asks: Joseph had waited quietly for the kingdom of God, and when the moment came, he acted. The women watched, and then rested, and then got up early. Ask whether you are waiting for God in a way that will be ready to act when it costs something. Sometimes faithfulness is brave, and sometimes it is simply coming with spices at dawn.
